title: What is common between fractions greater than one?
description: The black fractions that are greater than one are compared with the blue fractions that are less than one. The board looks at the top and bottom number of each and links the pattern to the parts that fill a whole. Keeko doubts that five fifths is more than one.
teaching_notes: One idea: a fraction is greater than one when it has more parts than the bottom number says make a whole. Watch for students who say a fraction with equal top and bottom numbers is more than one.

source: Did you notice something common between the fractions that are greater than 1?
video_script.why: A learner sees that a fraction is greater than one when its top number is larger than its bottom number.
video_script.substitution: the book's own black and blue fractions from the number lines
video_script.anchor: the two groups of fractions from the earlier number lines
video_script.wrong_answer: five fifths is more than one, because the top is not smaller than the bottom
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko reads equal top and bottom numbers as past one, though five fifths ends exactly at the mark one.
video_script.payoff_line: In fractions greater than one, the top number is larger than the bottom number

final_answer.value: In fractions greater than 1 the numerator is larger than the denominator; in fractions less than 1 the numerator is smaller than the denominator.
final_answer.spoken: in fractions greater than one the top number is larger than the bottom number, and in fractions less than one it is smaller

video_script.fraction_reading: three halves, six fifths, seven fifths, eight fifths, nine fifths, two thirds, four fifths, five fifths
hold_back: the top number is larger than the bottom number
maths_rules: greater than 1: 3/2, 6/5, 7/5, 8/5, 9/5 have the top number larger than the bottom number
less than 1: 2/3, 4/5 have the top number smaller than the bottom number
the bottom number says how many equal parts make 1 whole, so more parts than that go past 1
video_script.design: The two groups of fractions side by side with the top and bottom numbers coloured. A unit bar shows when the parts pass one whole.

<bookmark mark='groups'/>The black fractions are more than one unit, and the blue fractions are less than one unit.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What is common between the fractions that are greater than one?

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='top'/>The top number of a fraction is called the numerator.
<bookmark mark='bottom'/>The bottom number is called the denominator.
<bookmark mark='whole'/>The bottom number also tells how many equal parts make one whole.

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the black fractions are three halves, six fifths, seven fifths, eight fifths and nine fifths.

beats.on_screen: To find: what is common between the fractions greater than 1
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find what is common between the fractions that are greater than one.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: black fractions. 3/2: top 3, bottom 2. 6/5: top 6, bottom 5

marks.fifth: six fifths is shown with its top number six and its bottom number five

beats.colours: top number = one colour, bottom number = a second colour
narration: <bookmark mark='black'/>Step one, look at the black fractions.
<bookmark mark='half'/>In three halves, the top number is three and the bottom number is two.
<bookmark mark='fifth'/>In six fifths, the top number is six and the bottom number is five.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: blue fractions. 2/3: top 2, bottom 3. 4/5: top 4, bottom 5

marks.third: two thirds is shown with its top number two and its bottom number three
marks.fifth: four fifths is shown with its top number four and its bottom number five

beats.colours: top number = one colour, bottom number = a second colour
narration: <bookmark mark='blue'/>Step two, now look at the blue fractions.
<bookmark mark='third'/>In two thirds, the top number is two and the bottom number is three.
<bookmark mark='fifth'/>In four fifths, the top number is four and the bottom number is five.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: the bottom number = parts in 1 whole; 7/5 = 7 parts, but 5 parts fill the unit

marks.extra: two more parts of seven fifths go past the mark one

narration: <bookmark mark='why'/>Step three, the bottom number is how many parts fill one whole. Five parts fill the unit when the bottom number is five.
<bookmark mark='extra'/>Seven fifths has seven parts, so two parts go past one.

beats.on_screen: Check: 4/5 has 4 parts, 1 part short of the whole; 8/5 has 8 parts, past the whole

marks.check: four fifths stops one part before the mark one, and eight fifths goes past it

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>To check, four fifths has fewer than five parts, so it stops short of one. Eight fifths has more than five parts, so it goes past one.

beats.on_screen: Answer: greater than 1: the top number is larger than the bottom number; less than 1: the top number is smaller than the bottom number

marks.ans: the first rule is boxed beside the black box
marks.less: the second rule is written beside the blue box

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>In fractions greater than one, the top number is larger than the bottom number.
<bookmark mark='less'/>In fractions less than one, the top number is smaller than the bottom number.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the two boxes
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a bubble says 5/5 is more than 1 because the top is not smaller than the bottom; a bar of five parts ends exactly at the mark 1; the bubble is struck out

marks.doubt: the bubble with the wrong idea appears
marks.fill: a unit bar of five parts is shaded and it ends exactly at the mark one
marks.fix: the bubble is struck out and five fifths is written as equal to one

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks five fifths is more than one, because the top is not smaller than the bottom.
<bookmark mark='fill'/>Shade five fifths. Five parts exactly fill the unit, and the line ends at one.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Five fifths is equal to one. For more than one, the top number must be larger.
